topic: Solving systems algebraically by substitution or elimination
subtitle: Substitution, elimination, and choosing between them

problems.desc: Part (b): justification of the method chosen for the ticket system. Full credit requires the student to say that both equations already contain the same child-ticket term, 3 times the child price, so subtracting one equation from the other removes it in a single step, while substitution would first require solving one equation for a variable and would bring in fractions. Accept an answer that only points out the matching terms as the reason elimination is quicker.

Part (b): justification of the method chosen for the two gym costs. Full credit requires the student to say that both equations are already solved for the cost, so the two expressions can be set equal to each other straight away, which is substitution in its quickest form. Accept an answer that says elimination would work but needs an extra rearranging step first.

Part (b): explanation of what a system with no solution means for the two catering claims. Full credit requires the student to say that doubling the first order gives 4 trays of fruit and 6 of bread for 92 dollars, which contradicts the quoted 100 dollars, so the two claims cannot both be true and no pair of prices satisfies them. Accept an answer that notes the second equation is the first multiplied by 2 on the left but not on the right. Do not accept 'no solution' with no reference to the two orders.

Part (b): justification of the first move on the boat-and-current system. Full credit requires the student to say that the current term appears as plus c in one equation and minus c in the other, so simply adding the two equations cancels it and leaves the boat speed at once. Accept an answer that also notes subtracting the equations would isolate the current speed just as quickly.
